 Some Brad's Crunchy Kale and Veggie Chips Recalled Due to Heavy Metal Contamination
 The snacks have elevated levels of thallium, according to the California Department of Public Health
 By 
 Lisa L. Gill 
 Investigative Reporter 
 November 6, 2026 
 Four varieties of Brad's Crunchy snacks were listed in the FDA recall notice. The California Department of Public Health advised consumers to avoid four additional varieties as well, also due to potential thallium contamination.
 Photo: Brad's Raw Chips
 Four varieties of Brad’s Crunchy Kale and Veggie chips were recalled by the manufacturer, Snack Right Super Foods, because they could be contaminated with thallium, a heavy metal that can be harmful if it accumulates in your body over time. Recalled products were sold in stores nationwide, including at Whole Foods , and online. 
 Thallium toxicity can cause hair loss, numbness and pain in the feet and hands, diarrhea, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and heart problems, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention .

 The Food and Drug Administration recall notice cites four products (see list below). However, four additional Brad’s Crunchy products were the subject of an alert in March by the California Department of Public Health, which noted that they should not be consumed due to the thallium contamination risk. The CDPH told CR that it “remains concerned about the Brad’s products that were not included in the recall and continues to advise consumers not to consume these products.” (CDPH does not have the authority to issue a mandatory recall.)
 Snack Right Super Foods did not answer our questions about why only four of the eight products subject to the alert in California were recalled, which retailers sold the products, or why the company initially refused a recall. The FDA also did not respond to CR’s questions about the additional products CDPH identified as having elevated levels of thallium and why those were not recalled, or why the company was allowed to refuse a recall back in March when it was first informed of the elevated thallium levels.

 These four additional Brad's products were cited by the California Department of Public Health in an alert advising consumers to avoid them due to potential thallium contamination.
 Photo: Brad's Raw Chips 
 Photo: Brad's Raw Chips 
 These additional products were cited in the CDPH’s alert, though additional information about lot codes and expiration dates was not provided:
 Brad’s Crunchy Kale Vampire Killer  
 Brad’s Balsamic Salad Snack  
 Brad’s Ranch Salad Snack 
 Brad’s Crunchy Kale Nacho  
 If you have any of these items, throw them away. The company is not offering a refund. Contact Snack Right Super Foods with questions by email , Monday through Friday, 10:00 a.m. to 4:00 p.m. EST.
 The thallium contamination was discovered after a consumer alerted California public health officials to an elevated level of thallium in their urine. The CDPH said in its release that after receiving the consumer complaint it collected samples at retail stores in the Sacramento area, tested the products, and found elevated thallium levels in multiple varieties of the product. CDPH told CR that the consumer reported eating Brad’s kale chips almost daily for over a year.
 The Risks of Thallium
 Thallium is a naturally occurring metal found in soil and water and can also contaminate the environment through the burning of coal and the production of cement. It can be absorbed by plants growing in the ground (as well as by fish in lakes or the ocean). The FDA’s release states that plants such as kale are known to accumulate certain elements, such as thallium, from soil. 
 The dehydration process used to make the recalled snacks removed most of the water from kale and other vegetables, leaving behind a concentrated amount of thallium, according to the FDA’s release. 
 If you have symptoms of thallium toxicity , contact your doctor to obtain a hair or urine test.
 Because kids might eat these snacks, James E. Rogers, PhD, director of food safety testing at CR, reminds parents that it’s important to feed children a variety of foods, as they can be especially vulnerable to contaminated products. “Switch up the foods children eat to avoid overconsumption of any one food or spice,” he says.
 When possible, you can also minimize your family’s exposure to heavy metals by testing your water for lead and arsenic and, if levels are high, installing a water filter . For babies and young children, see CR’s advice on choosing formulas and baby foods low in heavy metals.
 Lisa L. Gill
 Lisa L. Gill is an award-winning investigative reporter. She has been at Consumer Reports since 2008, covering health and food safety—heavy metals in the food supply and foodborne illness—plus healthcare and prescription drug costs, medical debt, and credit scores. Lisa also testified before Congress and the Food and Drug Administration about her work on drug costs and drug safety. She lives in a DIY tiny home, where she gardens during the day and stargazes the Milky Way at night.
